title: The Battle Before The Battle
subtitle: Shooting the Messenger
tagline: The person who exposes a problem is not necessarily the person who created it.
headline: Shooting the Messenger
headline_sub: When the Truth-Teller Becomes the Problem
seo_title: Shooting the Messenger: When Truth-Tellers Get Blamed
seo_description: Ahab called Elijah the troubler of Israel. How leaders and organizations turn the person who raises a concern into the problem, and how to give truth a fair hearing.
og_image_alt: Shooting the Messenger: The person who exposes a problem is not necessarily the person who created it. TheWrkShop, Leadership & Culture.

scriptures.text: When he saw Elijah, he said to him, “Is that you, you troubler of Israel?” “I have not made trouble for Israel,” Elijah replied. “But you and your father’s family have. You have abandoned the LORD’s commands and have followed the Baals.”

Then the officials said to the king, “This man should be put to death. He is discouraging the soldiers who are left in this city, as well as all the people, by the things he is saying to them. This man is not seeking the good of these people but their ruin.”

blocks.text: Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel. Elijah answers that Ahab and his father’s house brought the trouble by abandoning God’s commands.
In Jeremiah 38, officials accuse Jeremiah of weakening the people’s resolve because his message contradicts the course they prefer.
Notice what Ahab does.
He sees Elijah and immediately assigns blame.
The prophet becomes the problem.
But Elijah reverses the accusation.
The trouble didn’t begin with the person who exposed the disobedience.
It began with the disobedience itself.
THE PERSON WHO REVEALS A PROBLEM IS NOT NECESSARILY THE PERSON WHO CREATED IT.
Jeremiah faces the same danger.
His message is unwelcome.
Officials argue that his words undermine morale.
Instead of seriously weighing his warning, they try to silence him.
That’s what makes these accounts so sobering.
A leader can become more disturbed by the disclosure of trouble than by the trouble being disclosed.
“IF THIS PERSON WOULD STOP TALKING, WE COULD MOVE FORWARD.”
Imagine an employee reporting a serious concern.
Instead of examining the evidence, leadership starts discussing the employee’s attitude.

items: Why couldn’t they handle this privately?
Why are they making everyone uncomfortable?

blocks.text: The original concern slowly disappears.
The conversation becomes about the person who raised it.
WHEN THE MESSENGER BECOMES THE INVESTIGATION, THE MESSAGE MAY NEVER GET A FAIR HEARING.
What makes an uncomfortable truth feel so threatening?
Usually one quiet question underneath it all:
What if it’s true?
If it’s true, something will have to change. Reputations may suffer. Someone we trust may have failed. We may have missed it.
It’s easier to question the messenger than to sit with that.
To be fair, not every accusation is accurate.
Not every critic is trustworthy.
Not every disagreement is prophetic courage.
That’s why evidence, fairness, confidentiality, and a proper investigation matter.
But those protections must apply to everyone.
They cannot become excuses to dismiss concerns before examining them.
THE BATTLE BEGINS WHEN PROTECTING OUR REPUTATION FEELS MORE URGENT THAN DISCOVERING WHAT IS TRUE.
TRUTH SHOULD NOT HAVE TO PASS A LOYALTY TEST BEFORE IT RECEIVES A FAIR HEARING.
A healthy organization separates the substance of a concern from assumptions about the person raising it.

items: It takes appropriate action when the evidence warrants it.

blocks.text: And it does not confuse peace with the absence of uncomfortable conversations.
Biblical peace is not maintained by concealing what needs correction.

items: When someone reports harm, do we examine the evidence or focus on why they spoke?
Are concerns evaluated differently depending on the influence of the person involved?
Can someone question a decision without being labeled divisive?
What happened to the last person who raised a difficult concern?
Have we made speaking truth more costly than hiding a problem?

blocks.text: Examine how concerns are received.
And resist the temptation to defend a conclusion before the facts are known.
The person who exposes a problem is not necessarily the person who created it.

Father, give us courage to hear difficult truth. Protect us from defensiveness, suspicion, and injustice. Help us examine concerns fairly, protect those who are vulnerable, and respond faithfully to what is revealed. May truth matter more than appearance. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
The messenger may be uncomfortable without being wrong.
Silencing a warning does not remove the danger.
Truth should not require personal popularity to receive a fair hearing.
An organization reveals its character by how it handles inconvenient information.
—TheWrkShop
